references.text: Jesus gives the same teaching to the disciples that whoever wants to be great among them must be a servant to others. [ref:Matt 20:25-28|Matthew 20:25-28] contains the parallel where Jesus contrasts the ruling style of Gentile nations with the servant leadership he calls the disciples to.

Jesus says that whoever is greatest among you must be your servant, and that whoever exalts themselves will be humbled ([ref:Matt 23:11-12|Matthew 23:11-12]). This emphasizes the same principle of humble service as a mark of true greatness.

Mark's parallel to this teaching where Jesus says that whoever wants to become great among you must be everyone's servant, and that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve ([ref:Mark 10:42-45|Mark 10:42-45]).
Jesus demonstrates servant leadership in practice by washing the disciples' feet ([ref:Joh 13:4-5|John 13:4-5]), which is a concrete action illustrating the principle that leaders must serve.
After the foot washing, Jesus explains that as Lord and Teacher he has given them an example, and that they should do likewise to one another ([ref:Joh 13:13-15|John 13:13-15]).

Paul urges humility and putting others above oneself, with Christ as the model – he who had the form of God but took on the form of a servant ([ref:Fil 2:3-8|Philippians 2:3-8]). This expands on the theology behind Jesus' words about servant leadership.

Peter exhorts elders not to lord it over those entrusted to them, but to be examples to the flock, and the young to submit to the older, and all to clothe themselves with humility ([ref:1 Pet 5:3-5|1 Peter 5:3-5]). This reflects Jesus' teaching on humble service in leadership.
An earlier statement by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke that whoever is the least among you all, he is great ([ref:Luk 9:48|Luke 9:48]). The same principle that true greatness is found in humility.
